new_statements.quote: With regard to stress, the prefixes are part of the same word as the stem and the suffixes: Chintang words contain one main stress, and it regularly falls onto the last syllable of the lexical stem (and the first stem in compounds). Prefixes are never stressed, since they are not stems. There is evidence, however, that the prefixes form phonological subconstituents on their own within the word. In the following representation of this, ω2 denotes a level between the phonological word and the phonological phrase, and is the domain for stress assignment [...] (22) ( ω2 ( ω pf/Σ1) ( ω Σ(′)-sf))
new_statements.citation: Bickel, Balthasar, Goma Banjade, Martin Gaenszle, Elena Lieven, Netra P. Paudyal, Ichchha Purna Rai, Manoj Rai, Novel Kishore Rai & Sabine Stoll. 2007. Free prefix ordering in Chintang. Language 83(1): 43-73.
new_statements.locator: §4.2 Phonological wordhood, p. 56 (PDF p. 14 of 31); domain summary §4.3, p. 57 ex. (31)
new_statements.rule_in_words: One main stress per word; it falls on the last syllable of the lexical stem (in compounds, on the first stem). Prefixes are never stressed, and the suffixes that follow the stem are not stressed either, so the position is fixed relative to the stem edge, not to the word edge. The stress domain (ω2) is the whole grammatical word: prefixes + stem + suffixes, and it also hosts enclitics.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds: stress goes to the first stem. Separately, in the Mundum ritual language, binomial 'limbs' each take stress on their first syllable (Vorberg et al. 2009, p. 5, citing Rai 2007) — a register-specific pattern, not a statement about everyday word stress. Dirksmeyer 2008 notes demonstratives huŋ/ba can carry their own primary stress under contrastive use.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the domain of stress assignment is the phonological word ω2 = prefixes + stem(s) + suffixes (the grammatical word), also the host domain for enclitics. The source is a morphology paper on prefix ordering (Language), not a phonology description; the stress statement is a brief one-sentence characterization with no stress-marked examples, although its main claims are corroborated second-hand by Schiering & van der Hulst 2010: 586-587 ('one primary accent which regularly falls on the last syllable of the lexical stem').
new_statements.identity_note: Chintang proper (chhi1245), the variety of Chhintang VDC, Dhankuta District, documented by the Chintang and Puma Documentation Project / Chintang Language Research Program (Bickel, Stoll, Gaenszle, N. K. Rai). The 2007 paper does not name a sub-dialect; Dirksmeyer 2008 mentions two village dialects (Mulgaũ vs. Sambugaũ) differing in minor forms. Not to be confused with Bantawa (bant1281), of which Chintang was once treated as a dialect.
